questions.question: What is mypy and how do you use it for static type checking in Python?
questions.title: Static Type Checking with mypy
questions.direct_answer: mypy is a static type checker that analyses Python source and type hints without executing the program. Install it as a development dependency, run `mypy` against the package, fix or configure reported mismatches, and run it in local checks and CI so typed contracts stay consistent.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand static analysis, annotations, configuration, CI use, and the boundary with runtime behaviour.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting mypy to run automatically with Python or assuming a successful check proves runtime input is valid.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention gradual typing and explain why strictness should be recorded in project configuration rather than personal command history.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: mypy reads code and annotations without running the application.
Run it explicitly, for example with `mypy src` or `python -m mypy src`.
It checks typed functions, their calls, assignments, and return paths.
Store options in `pyproject.toml` or `mypy.ini` and run the same check in CI.
A clean mypy result does not replace tests or runtime validation.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
mypy is a static type checker for Python. It reads source code and annotations, infers additional types, and reports inconsistent calls, assignments, operations, or return values without starting the application.

I install it as a development tool and run it against the real package, for example `python -m mypy src`. I keep the selected Python version, package paths, plugins, and strictness options in `pyproject.toml` or `mypy.ini` so every developer and CI uses the same rules.

For example, if `greet(name: str) -> str` is called as `greet(42)`, mypy can report the incompatible argument before that path is executed. It can also catch a function that promises `str` but returns an integer.

mypy supports gradual typing, so a project can begin with important models and public boundaries and expand coverage over time. Untyped code and `Any` reduce what it can prove, so I make those gaps visible and tighten them deliberately.

Running mypy never makes Python enforce hints at runtime. I still need tests for behaviour and parsing or validation for external values; mypy protects consistency among the code paths it can analyse.

sections.title: A second pass over the program
sections.content:
The Python interpreter executes objects and operations. mypy performs a separate analysis pass: it builds a type for each checked expression, follows control flow, resolves imports and stubs, and compares actual uses with declared contracts. Because it does not need a branch to run, it can inspect rare error paths before a test reaches them.

Configuration defines the analysis boundary. The target Python version determines which syntax and standard-library features are available. Import settings decide how much is known about dependencies. Strictness options decide whether unannotated definitions, implicit optional values, unused ignores, and forms of `Any` should be reported.

A repeatable workflow treats type checking like tests and linting: run it quickly during development, use a stable configuration, and make CI reject new violations. Inline ignores should be narrow and explained because they remove checking at exactly the line where uncertainty exists.

sections.title: Where mypy fits in development
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[Python source and type hints] --> M[mypy analysis]
  C[Project configuration and stubs] --> M
  M -->|mismatch| E[Developer fixes code, hint, or narrow config]
  E --> M
  M -->|clean| CI[Same command in CI]
  CI --> R[Python still runs dynamically]
  R --> T[Tests and runtime validation]
```

sections.title: Keep the executable example valid while exposing a checker case
sections.content:
```python
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name}"

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    greet(42)  # mypy checks this block and reports an incompatible argument

print(greet("Ada"))
```

`TYPE_CHECKING` is false at runtime but treated as true by static checkers, so the program runs safely while the example still demonstrates mypy's diagnostic.

questions.question: How do you introduce mypy gradually into an existing Python project?
questions.title: Adopting mypy Without a Big-Bang Rewrite
questions.direct_answer: Add mypy to CI with a shared configuration, start with high-value boundaries or a small package, and expand the checked surface in measurable steps. Keep temporary exceptions narrow, prevent regressions in already-typed code, and raise strictness as missing annotations and `Any` values are removed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can adopt static checking safely in a real codebase instead of demanding an all-at-once conversion.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Enabling strict mode across a large legacy repository, receiving thousands of errors, and then globally suppressing useful checks.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Prioritize widely imported modules and external boundaries so each new annotation provides information to many callers.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Commit one shared mypy configuration and run it in CI.
Begin with a small package, public API, or widely imported model layer.
Make new or changed code meet the stronger standard immediately.
Keep per-module exceptions temporary and avoid broad global ignores.
Track remaining untyped definitions and `Any` sources as migration work.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I introduce mypy as an incremental quality gate rather than trying to annotate the entire repository in one change. First I commit a configuration with the project's Python version and a command that runs identically on developer machines and in CI.

I start where type information has the widest effect: shared data models, public service functions, utility modules with many callers, and adapters around external data. For example, typing one widely used parser can give precise results to dozens of checked callers.

Existing weak areas can receive narrow per-module settings while new and modified modules follow a stronger rule such as disallowing untyped definitions. I avoid a global `ignore_missing_imports` or large collections of unexplained `# type: ignore` comments because they can hide unrelated errors.

I then shrink the exception list, annotate one dependency direction at a time, and use tools such as `reveal_type` to find where `Any` enters. The CI check prevents completed areas from going backwards.

Strict mode can be the destination, but the useful goal is steadily increasing trustworthy coverage. Tests and runtime validation continue alongside the migration because static checking addresses a different class of failure.

sections.title: Expand a typed island along dependency edges
sections.content:
Type information becomes more useful as it crosses module boundaries. Starting with a leaf script may find local mistakes, but a precise model or helper imported by many modules supplies facts to the whole dependency graph. This is why widely imported definitions and input parsers are strong first targets.

Gradual adoption needs a ratchet: the accepted baseline may contain gaps, but a checked area should not silently become untyped again. Per-module configuration can describe temporary differences without weakening unrelated packages. Error-code-specific ignores make the remaining exception visible and reviewable.

Third-party packages may provide inline hints or stub packages. When no useful types exist, a small local adapter can contain the unknown values and return a validated typed model. This is safer than allowing `Any` from one import to spread through the application.

sections.title: A migration that tightens over time
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  B[Record baseline configuration] --> H[Type one high-value boundary]
  H --> C[Run mypy in CI]
  C --> N[Require stronger rules for new code]
  N --> S[Shrink per-module exceptions]
  S --> M[Expand to dependent modules]
  M --> C
```

questions.question: Why can mypy miss errors in untyped functions or values marked Any?
questions.title: How Untyped Code and Any Limit mypy
questions.direct_answer: mypy is intentionally gradual: by default, a completely unannotated function is treated as dynamically typed, and `Any` permits almost any operation and assignment. Those choices create holes in static analysis, so annotate function boundaries and use stricter options to reveal accidental `Any` values.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand why adding mypy alone does not automatically check every line in a legacy project.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating `Any` as an ordinary top type or using it to silence a diagnostic without recognizing that checking is being disabled.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast `Any` with `object` and name `check_untyped_defs`, `disallow_untyped_defs`, and `reveal_type` as diagnostic tools.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A fully unannotated function is dynamically typed under mypy's normal gradual model.
`Any` allows nearly every operation and can flow into other variables unnoticed.
`object` requires narrowing before type-specific operations and is safer for unknown values.
Use `reveal_type` to locate where precision was lost.
Stricter options can check untyped bodies and reject new untyped definitions or bare generics.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
mypy supports gradual typing, so it does not assume that every old Python function is fully typed. A function with no annotations is normally treated as dynamically typed, and many mistakes inside it are not reported under the default configuration.

`Any` creates a similar gap inside typed code. A checker permits almost every attribute access, call, assignment, and operation on an `Any` value, and results derived from it often remain `Any`.

For example, an untyped JSON helper may return `Any`; calling a misspelled method on that result can pass mypy and then fail in production. If the value is typed as `object` instead, code must use `isinstance` or another validator before string-specific operations are allowed.

I use `reveal_type` during analysis to locate the first place a precise type became `Any`. Options such as `check_untyped_defs`, `disallow_untyped_defs`, and `disallow_any_generics` can expose different sources of missing coverage.

Some `Any` is practical at difficult library boundaries, but I keep it local and convert it into a validated typed value. A successful mypy run is only as strong as the annotations, stubs, and configuration it analysed.

sections.title: Any is an escape hatch, not an unknown object
sections.content:
`Any` participates in assignments in both directions: a value of `Any` can be assigned where a precise type is expected, and a precise value can be stored as `Any`. Operations on it are also accepted. This flexibility enables gradual migration and dynamic integration, but it stops the checker from proving the local behaviour.

`object` means every Python value is allowed, yet only operations shared by all objects are initially safe. A runtime check narrows it to a useful type. That makes `object` the better default when the program truly receives an unknown value and intends to inspect it safely.

Untyped functions are another entrance for implicit `Any`. Adding at least the boundary annotations lets mypy check the body with useful information. `reveal_type` is a checker-only diagnostic that displays its current inference; it helps trace a weak third-party stub, a bare generic, or an unannotated call back to its source.

sections.title: How Any spreads a blind spot
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U[Untyped function or weak stub] --> A[Any result]
  A --> O[Arbitrary operation accepted]
  O --> A2[Another Any result]
  A2 --> P[Assigned into precise-looking code]
  X[object result] --> N[isinstance or validation]
  N --> T[Precise narrowed type]
```
